deep.reconstruction:
This page has no derivation. It is a verbatim French excerpt that Riemann copied from G. Lamé, 'Leçons sur la théorie mathématique de l'élasticité des corps solides' (Paris 1852). The folio carries the archival label 'Riemann 18'. The next page is headed 'Excerpte aus Lamé' and gives the earlier page references (pp. 11, 35–38). The opening lines here finish Lamé's p. 38 remark (Leçon III, §15): the method going back to Cauchy 'is beyond objection'. It does not assume continuity of matter, and it leaves the number of molecular pairs contributing to the elastic force undetermined.

The second passage is Lamé p. 76, Leçon VI, §30. It sums up why his route to the general equations of elasticity is better than Navier's and Poisson's 'integration around a point'.

(a) The older approach expresses the elastic constants through integrals of an unknown intermolecular force function f(ζ) times powers of ζ. My gloss: these are typically of the form ∫ f(ζ) ζ^n dζ. Debates over the form of f and the relative size of such integrals are declared pointless. Lamé assumes only that f(ζ) is negligible ('insensible') once ζ is sensible, i.e. forces are of molecular range only.

(b) Integration around a point presupposes continuity of matter, which Lamé calls absurd. He replaces it with continuity of the geometric displacements (his §11).

(c) Homogeneous solids of constant elasticity (isotropic bodies) need no vague averaging of molecular spacings. Lamé's §§17 and 20 show a molecular arrangement can exist that is symmetric about certain planes and deforms the same way under traction or torsion in any direction.

(d) The old method forces λ = μ. My gloss: these are the Cauchy relations of the 'rari-constant' theory, which give Poisson ratio 1/4, and experiment contradicts the resulting formulas. In Lamé's theory λ and μ are independent and their ratio is left undetermined.

(e) Rhetorical close: the old theory rested on hypotheses, the new one on facts.

In modern terms the page argues for linear isotropic elasticity with two independent Lamé constants:
σ = λ tr(ε) I + 2μ ε,
leading to Navier–Lamé equations
(λ+μ) grad div u + μ Δu = 0,
as against the one-constant (λ = μ) molecular theory of Navier and Poisson. Riemann adds no commentary of his own on this page.
errors: No errors by Riemann; this is a copied excerpt.

On Lamé's own argument: the equality λ = μ does not come from the continuum 'integration around a point' as such. It follows from assuming central pairwise molecular forces with no initial stress, and Cauchy's discrete lattice sums give the same Cauchy relations. Lamé's two independent constants come from dropping the specific central-force hypothesis, not from avoiding continuity. His diagnosis is therefore historically and physically partial.

results.what: Critique of Navier–Poisson molecular derivation (integration around a point, unknown force law f(ζ)) and its consequence λ = μ
results.modern_name: Rari-constant vs multi-constant controversy; Cauchy relations (Poisson ratio 1/4)
results.usually_credited_to: Navier (1821/27), Poisson (1829), Cauchy (1828); critique by Green (1839), Lamé (1852), Stokes

results.what: Isotropic elasticity with two independent constants λ, μ

deep.surprise_reason: This is a reading excerpt copied verbatim from Lamé's 1852 Leçons, with no original mathematics. It documents only Riemann's reading for his natural-philosophy studies, which is already known.

checkable.asserts: With λ = μ (Navier–Poisson), Poisson's ratio ν = λ/(2(λ+μ)) equals 1/4.
With λ = μ, Young's modulus E = μ(3λ+2μ)/(λ+μ) equals 5μ/2; this is the one-constant relation that experiment (e.g. Wertheim) contradicted.

Line 'est ou petit, ou grand': the image reads roughly 'est ou petits ou grand'. This is a minor slip of the pen; the meaning is unchanged.
'établi des formules': the image runs the words together as 'établides formules'.
